growth.juvenile_note: Tiny epigeal seedlings on moss grow only 2.5-15 cm a year. Saplings are narrow, spindly spires with short blue-green needles and a dense, club-like top; lower branches drooping onto the moss often root (layering), ringing an old tree with young clones. Mature trees look like bottle-brushes with a knob of cones at the top.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Viereck & Johnston): seedlings 2.5 cm/yr on moss, to 15 cm on mineral soil; 12-20 m on good sites; main cone-bearing age 30-250; establishes in 10% of full light; layering common; average max age ~200, up to 280 years

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (pollen late May-early June; cones 1-4 cm, green or purplish when young, seed mature late Aug-early Sep; semi-serotinous cones stay partly closed on the tree for years, holding viable seed up to 25 years and releasing it gradually or after fire; heavy crops every 2-6 years)

canopy.name: Jack pine
canopy.origin: Boreal Canada and the Great Lakes

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 3-5 cotyledons that needs bare mineral soil or ash, typically after fire. Young trees grow fast into narrow, open cones with short, stiff, twisted paired needles; they bear cones within a few years, and the curved, closed cones stay on the branches for decades. Old trees are scraggly, with crooked limbs, an open irregular crown and many dead lower branches.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 1 (Rudolph & Laidly): germination within weeks on burned seedbeds; cones on open-grown trees at 3-5 years, abundant crops from about 10; 17-20 m on good sites; very intolerant of shade; seldom lives beyond 150 years, maximum about 230

canopy.source: Canadian boreal; 15–25 m. Fire-sealed cones; poor sandy ground. Kew POWO for the name; standard floras for range.

fruit.form: curved, lopsided cones 3-5 cm pointing forward along the branch, sealed with resin and held closed for years until fire opens them

canopy.name: Lodgepole pine

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 3-6 cotyledons and a tuft of single primary needles, then short, twisted, paired needles. Young trees are dense, narrow cones with regular whorls. Open-grown shore pines become bushy, crooked and flat-topped; inland trees become slim, straight poles. Serotinous cones stay closed on the branches for decades.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Lotan & Critchfield): viable seed commonly at 5-10 years; ~3.6 m at 20 years on medium sites; germination peaks in the 2 weeks after snowmelt; very intolerant of shade; shore pine small and short-lived; ages commonly 150-200+, old high-elevation trees to 400+

canopy.name: White spruce

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 6-7 cotyledons, very slow at first (often under 10 cm after two years in the forest). Saplings are neat, dense, narrow cones of stiff blue-green needles in regular whorls, keeping their lower branches; older trees become tall, narrow spires with slightly drooping side branches and a pointed top.

growth.source: USDA FEIS Rosa acicularis (0.3-1.2 m, up to 3 m; spreads by rhizomes and sprouts vigorously after fire; seeds need warm then cold stratification and may wait a year or more; flowers June-July). Ages estimated

ground.name: Feather moss

growth.juvenile_note: A spore germinates into a green, thread-like protonema on humus or rotten wood that buds small leafy shoots. These become loose, glossy yellow-green, once-pinnate feathery shoots on conspicuous red stems with blunt, crowded leaves, adding roughly 1-2 cm a year and weaving into a springy carpet 3-10 cm deep. Most new patches start from broken shoot fragments.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.name: Stair-step moss

growth.juvenile_note: Young plants are small loose wefts of red-stemmed, feathery, olive to golden-green fronds creeping over humus, logs or rock. Each year a new frond arches up from the middle of last year's, so a shoot becomes a staircase of flat, fern-like steps, one per year, the oldest dying brown underneath. A deep carpet rebuilds only slowly after fire, once a canopy has closed.
growth.source: Trees for Life (new segment each year from the centre of the previous one, segments live up to ~8 yr, sporophytes uncommon, slow recolonisation after fire, shade-loving); Wikipedia (one step per year used to age shoots). appearance.silhouette: fine bright-green tufts with a silvery-purple haze of flowers
appearance.refs: Flora of North America vol. 24 (Avenella flexuosa); Online Atlas of the British and Irish Flora

associations.name: Spruce-fir feathermoss forest
associations.where: mesic mid-slopes and moist loamy flats, sheltered
associations.source: Cajander 1926 forest site types (Myrtillus type); La Roi 1967 boreal spruce forests

associations.name: Scots pine lichen woodland
associations.where: dry sandy ridges, eskers and outwash plains, fire-prone

associations.name: Black spruce muskeg
associations.where: wet flats, peat basins and permafrost lowlands with standing water
associations.source: Viereck et al. 1992 Alaska Vegetation Classification; La Roi 1967

associations.name: Larch dwarf-birch open forest
associations.where: cold permafrost plains and north slopes of eastern Siberia
associations.source: Walter 1974 Vegetation of Eastern Europe and Northern Asia; Abaimov 2010

associations.name: Post-fire birch-fireweed stand
associations.where: recently burned ground and clearings, any slope
associations.source: Viereck 1973 Wildfire in the taiga of Alaska; Johnson 1992 Fire and Vegetation Dynamics
